Task 1: Proposed production architecture

Design proposal, 24 October 2026. Read alongside the as-built assessment. Existing application features are distinguished from proposed additions. No production features have been implemented.

Both target diagrams successfully validated and rendered through the connected Mermaid MCP. Returned PNG images are embedded below. The corrected sequence distinguishes confirmed transaction failure, confirmed commit and unknown commit outcome after a lost acknowledgement; it was successfully revalidated and rendered through Mermaid MCP. Sequence semicolons were escaped as #59; in the Mermaid source to correct syntax while preserving visible labels, architecture and evidence IDs. Validation confirms Mermaid syntax and rendering, not implementation or design correctness.

Design position

Persist approval, audit event and submission intent atomically in Azure SQL. A separate worker delivers committed intents to PayEx. The Task 2 decision record compares the three alternatives and recommends this design, subject to verification of PayEx capabilities.

The outbox prevents losing the intent between approval and delivery. It does not by itself guarantee exactly-once processing at PayEx. Approval, submission confirmation and payment settlement are separate concepts. The UI must never describe an invoice as paid solely because it was approved or a submission reference was received.

Legend: NEW means proposed and NOT IMPLEMENTED. Existing means supported by the cited code. Service Bus is a scenario resource, not an implemented application dependency.

2. Target approval and submission sequence

Open or edit validated diagram in Mermaid

The sequence follows an authorized request. The transaction has three outcomes: confirmed failure with rollback, confirmed durable commit, or unknown outcome after a lost acknowledgement. The unknown branch reads durable invoice and outbox state using the same operation identity before any retry; it never assumes rollback or creates a fresh submission key (T3, T4). The worker runs asynchronously and can process a committed intent while the API is still reconciling its lost acknowledgement; the browser may refresh while delivery is still Pending. Its placement after the worker branches is a presentation choice, not a requirement for the HTTP request to wait for PayEx. Existing 401 and 403 guards are retained as documented in the as-built sequence. All SQL transaction, worker, outbox and provider interactions shown below are proposed and not implemented.

Failure handling and operating implications

  • Use a conditional update or row-version comparison so only one concurrent decision commits. A uniqueness constraint permits one submission operation per approved invoice/version.
  • Snapshot the approved payload and derive a stable operation key. Retries reuse both. Do not mutate approved payment fields or create a new key to bypass uncertain outcomes.
  • Keep the external PayEx call outside the SQL transaction. A confirmed transaction failure rolls back approval, audit event and outbox intent. A confirmed commit makes all three durable. If the commit acknowledgement is lost, the outcome is unknown: read durable invoice and outbox state using the same operation identity before deciding whether to retry. A matching committed operation means return its current state without creating another intent. Retry only after the original transaction is definitively resolved as not committed and the invoice/version remains eligible; reuse the same operation identity, submission key and payload with conditional version checks and the uniqueness constraint. An unavailable read, an unresolved transaction or conflicting state requires reconciliation, not an assumed rollback or fresh key. T3, T4.
  • Persist worker leases and attempts. A crash after PayEx acceptance but before saving the response is the same uncertain-outcome problem as a timeout.
  • Only retry ambiguous sends after provider idempotency behavior and its retention window are verified, or evidence establishes that a resend is safe. Otherwise hold for operator reconciliation. This preserves caution about duplicates but cannot promise eventual delivery without a resolution process.
  • Track oldest pending age, unknown outcomes, terminal failures, lease recovery and audit-export gaps. Alert thresholds must follow the agreed SLO; the assignment does not supply an SLO value.
  • At 80 approvals per minute, a 30-second request duration implies roughly 40 simultaneous requests to sustain that rate in that scenario. This is a sizing estimate, not a benchmark. Verify provider limits, SQL behavior and worker concurrency under month-end load.
  • Application session storage is currently local to one process. Replica scaling and restart-safe authentication need a production identity/session design before rollout. No external identity provider has been selected or claimed implemented.

Agent inferences and unresolved assumptions

  1. The outbox, worker hosting arrangement, immutable audit archive and submission status model are proposed choices, not mandated architecture.
  2. Production identity, the numerical SLO, recovery objectives, PayEx contract and deployment replica counts are unverified.
  3. Seven-year retention requires operational controls and retrieval evidence. A SQL audit table alone is insufficient evidence of compliance.
  4. The worker and API may share an Azure platform but need independent scheduling and recovery. A specific worker hosting product has not been selected.
  5. The scenario's unused Service Bus and planned message topic are recorded separately from this proposal's direct outbox delivery; revisit if notification consumers require messaging.

3. Architecture rule and executable test

Rule: the compiled Domain assembly may reference only an explicit allow-list of .NET base libraries. Web, persistence and PayEx adapters must remain outside it. This keeps business decisions independent of infrastructure. The allow-list is deliberately restrictive; a legitimate new dependency requires review and an explicit update.

Test: DomainArchitectureTests.Domain_ReferencesOnlyDotNetBaseLibraries. It inspects assembly metadata rather than searching source text. It does not prove transaction safety, check dynamically loaded dependencies, or prohibit every inappropriate API within an allowed base library.

From the repository root:

dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln --filter FullyQualifiedName~DomainArchitectureTests
